title: The 2031 Car Plan — A Step-Up SIP, Built
tagline: Everything assembled into one concrete plan: a step-up SIP that funds Aarav's car down payment by 2031, on a strict 5-year horizon, balancing growth with capital protection.
summary: A specific step-up SIP plan and asset allocation to fund a car down payment in exactly 5 years.

sections.title: Step 1 — Define the goal in rupees

paragraphs: Aarav wants a car by 2031 — a strict 5-year horizon. The smart move for a first car on a modest income is to **fund the down payment** (and registration/insurance buffer) yourself, then take a small loan for the rest, which his by-then-strong CIBIL score (Module 3) will get at a good rate.

Assume a sensible entry car around **₹6–7 lakh on-road**. A healthy down payment of ~25–30% plus a buffer puts the savings target at roughly **₹2.5 lakh** by 2031. Funding more of the car yourself means a smaller loan and less interest — but never at the cost of draining the emergency fund.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Target a down payment of at least 20–30% of the car's price, keep the loan tenure short (≤5 years), and make sure the future EMI fits comfortably inside your budget. A car is a depreciating asset — minimise what you borrow for it.

sections.title: Step 2 — Choose the right vehicle for 5 years

paragraphs: Five years is a *medium* horizon (from the previous lesson). Pure equity is too risky for a fixed deadline; pure FD won't grow enough. So Aarav uses a **balanced mix with a glide path** — more growth early, shifting to safety as 2031 approaches.

items.term: ~50–60% in a Nifty 50 / broad index fund (Direct plan)
items.detail: The growth engine for the early years, when there's time to recover from dips.

items.term: ~40–50% in a short-duration debt fund or RD
items.detail: The stable anchor that limits how far the pot can fall.

items.term: Alternative: a single aggressive-hybrid or balanced-advantage fund
items.detail: One fund that auto-balances equity and debt — simpler for a beginner who doesn't want to manage two funds.

blocks.title: The glide path is non-negotiable
blocks.text: In year 4, start moving gains from equity into the debt/RD portion. By the last 6–12 months before 2031, the bulk should be in safe debt/FD so a market crash right before the purchase can't shrink the down payment. Lock in the win as the finish line nears.

sections.title: Step 3 — The step-up SIP, with numbers

paragraphs: A **step-up SIP** starts at an affordable amount and increases a set percentage each year as income grows — perfect for Aarav, who starts on ₹20,000 but expects raises. He begins at **₹3,000/month and steps up 10% every year.** At a balanced ~10% blended return, here's how the car fund builds:

blocks.title: ₹3,000/month, +10%/year, ~10% return
blocks.caption: Totals: ~₹2.20 lakh invested → ~₹2.78 lakh by end of year 5. Returns assumed, not guaranteed.

blocks.title: The result vs the goal
blocks.result: He clears the ₹2.5 lakh down-payment goal with a comfortable buffer — and the step-up means most of the heavy lifting came from modestly higher SIPs in the later years, funded by raises rather than belt-tightening.

blocks.title: Why step-up beats a flat SIP here
blocks.text: A flat ₹3,000 SIP for 5 years at 10% reaches only ~₹2.32 lakh — short of the goal. Stepping up 10%/year lifts him past ₹2.78 lakh without ever feeling a painful jump, because each increase lands when his income has (hopefully) grown too. Small annual increases, big end difference.

items.title: Emergency fund first, always
items.detail: The car SIP runs alongside — never instead of — the emergency fund. Don't raid the emergency fund for the down payment.

items.title: Keep this pot separate
items.detail: The car fund is its own SIP/folio, not mixed with retirement or emergency money, so the glide path and goal stay clear.

items.title: If the market is down in 2030, stay flexible
items.detail: Because of the glide path, most of the money is already safe by then. If equity is still weak, he can delay the purchase a few months or buy a slightly cheaper car — never panic-sell early.

items.title: Don't let the loan undo the discipline
items.detail: A bigger down payment from this fund means a smaller loan and less interest. Keep the EMI well within budget so the car never threatens the emergency fund or future SIPs.

blocks.text: This is goal-based investing end to end: a rupee target, an asset mix matched to a 5-year horizon, a step-up SIP sized to the income, a glide path to protect the finish, and guardrails so the rest of Aarav's financial life stays intact. Repeat this template for any future goal — a house, a wedding, higher studies.

cheatsheet: Define the goal in rupees first: ~₹2.5 lakh down payment for a ~₹6–7 lakh car by 2031.
5 years = medium horizon → balanced mix (~50–60% index + ~40–50% debt/RD), not pure equity.
Step-up SIP: start ₹3,000/month, +10%/year → ~₹2.78 lakh in 5 years at ~10% (clears the goal).
A flat ₹3,000 SIP reaches only ~₹2.32 lakh — stepping up makes the difference, funded by raises.
Glide path: shift from equity to debt/FD in years 4–5 so a late crash can't shrink the down payment.
Guardrails: emergency fund first, keep the car pot separate, stay flexible in 2030, keep the loan small.

questions.prompt: Why does Aarav use a balanced mix with a glide path for the car, rather than the aggressive all-equity approach recommended for his retirement money?
questions.hint: Compare 5 years to recover vs 38 years to recover.
answer: Because the car has a **fixed 5-year deadline** with little time to recover from a crash, while retirement is ~38 years away with plenty of time. Pure equity could be down 30% exactly in 2030–31, leaving him short for the car. A balanced mix limits that downside, and the glide path moves money to safety as 2031 nears so the down payment is protected.

Retirement money, by contrast, *should* be aggressive equity because decades of compounding outweigh any single crash. Same investor, different horizons, deliberately different strategies — which is the whole point of goal-based investing.
keyPoints: Glide path protects the finish line
Retirement (38 yr) can be aggressive equity

questions.prompt: A flat ₹3,000 SIP for 5 years reaches only ~₹2.32 lakh, but Aarav's step-up SIP reaches ~₹2.78 lakh. Where does the extra ~₹46,000 come from, and why doesn't it hurt his budget?
questions.hint: What changes each year in a step-up SIP, and what's also changing in his life?
answer: The extra comes from the **annual 10% increases** to the monthly SIP (₹3,000 → ₹3,300 → ₹3,630 …), which add more contributions in the later years plus the growth on them. More money invested, sooner-ish, compounding to a larger total.

It doesn't hurt his budget because the increases are timed to his expected raises — each step-up lands when his income has grown, so he never feels a painful jump. Small, gradual increases ride alongside rising income, which is exactly why step-up SIPs are so effective for someone early in their career.
keyPoints: Extra from annual 10% step-ups + their growth
No painful jump; gradual and affordable

questions.prompt: It's early 2031, the market just dropped 25%, and Aarav was about to buy the car. Because he followed the plan, why is he mostly fine — and what are his options?
questions.hint: What did the glide path do to his allocation by 2031?
answer: He's mostly fine because the **glide path** already moved the bulk of his car fund out of equity and into safe debt/FD during years 4–5. So a 25% equity drop hits only a small remaining equity sliver, not the whole down payment — the protected money is intact and predictable.

Options: (1) proceed with the purchase using the largely-safe corpus; (2) if a small part is still in equity and down, wait a few months for the deadline isn't truly rigid, or simply buy a slightly cheaper car; (3) never panic-sell the protected debt portion. The plan's design — separating the pot and de-risking near the finish — is exactly what turns a scary crash into a non-event.
keyPoints: Glide path already de-risked most of the fund
25% drop hits only a small equity sliver
Options: buy now, delay slightly, or buy cheaper
Design turns a crash into a non-event
